To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

non-synonymoussingle nucleotide variants explain 17% of the heritability attributable to low-frequency variants, and that the functional architectures of low-frequency variants and common variants are similar.

low-frequency variants are more enriched for heritability than common variants in cell-type-specific noncoding annotations, and that this enrichment can be used to estimate the mean effect size variance of rare variants in the annotation.

low-frequency variants are more enriched in functional non-coding annotations than common variants, and that this enrichment is driven by negative selection of low-frequency variants in functional annotations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the heritable genetic architecture of human traits and the functional annotation of non-coding variants.
how the heritability in complex traits is distributed across different genomic annotations and how this distribution relates to the functional architecture of the genome.
the functional annotation of genetic variants, with a specific focus on low frequency variants.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the functional architecture of low frequency variants is similar to common variants, but the functional architecture of rare variants is not well understood.
the functional architecture of low frequency variants is different than that of common variants, but that the differences are not as large as might have been predicted.

low-frequency variants are more strongly enriched in cell-type-specific noncoding annotations than common variants, but this enrichment is not as strong as the enrichment of common variants in cell-type-specific coding regions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
non-synonymus coding variants explain 2% of common heritability, but 17% of low-frequency heritability.
the strength of negative selection is the main determinant of functional enrichment of low-frequency and common variant heritabilities.
non-coding functional regions explain a greater proportion of low-frequency variant than common variant heritabilities.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the functional architecture of low-frequency and common variant heritabilities is very similar, with the notable exception that non-synonymuous low-frequency variants explain much more trait heritability than common variants.
low-frequency variants are enriched for functional annotations that are more strongly negatively selected than common variants, and this is true for both coding and non-coding annotations.

the heritability enrichment of low-frequency variants in cell-type-specific noncoding annotations depends on the mean strength of selection of causal variants in these annotations, and can be predicted by forward simulation.
